⚡ How to compare documents 🍿 Just a moment #02
Have you ever had to compare two versions of a complex document? What if one is a digital PDF and the other is a scan, spanning hundreds of pages, with different layouts and pagination? In this episode, see how Gemini's native multimodality spots subtle differences, from tiny typos to $100M contract updates, in a single prompt.

🍵 Grab your tea, coffee, or matcha… It only takes a moment!

Prompt template used in the video example:
[DOCUMENT_A]
…
[/DOCUMENT_A]
[DOCUMENT_B]
…
[/DOCUMENT_B]

TASK:
Perform an exhaustive, character-by-character textual comparison between DOCUMENT_A and DOCUMENT_B.

CRITICAL REQUIREMENTS:
1. You must systematically verify every numbered paragraph sequentially from start to finish.
2. You must catch every single difference, including single-character changes, minor typos, spelling corrections (e.g., missing letters in common words), and punctuation changes, in addition to substantive changes (numbers, dates, names).

OUTPUT FORMAT:
### Difference #[1, 2, 3…]
- Location: [location]
- Evidence A: "[short quote from Document A]" with difference in **bold**
- Evidence B: "[short quote from Document B]" with difference in **bold**
- Explanation: [brief description]

analysis.summary: A short AI Engineer talk from AWS's automated reasoning group introducing a Kiro specification analyzer that checks natural-language specs for conflicts, gaps and ambiguity before a coding agent writes code. The pipeline has an LLM refine wording, translate requirements into SMT-LIB formulas checked by a solver, then sample multiple translations and cluster them by logical equivalence to surface genuine ambiguity, which is escalated to the human as explicit options. The takeaway: the LLM translates, the solver checks, and the human decides, because only the user holds the domain knowledge to be the oracle for spec correctness.

description:

Your coding agent will faithfully build every one of them. Rajath Mahendrappa Kotyal shows how Kiro catches these before any design or code is generated by pairing LLMs with SMT solvers, turning the model's own disagreement into a signal that a requirement is ambiguous. You'll also see where solvers beat LLM-as-judge, and where they don't.

analysis.summary: Google Cloud Databases engineers Kurtis Van Gent (MCP core maintainer, transport WG lead) and Haoyu Wang present how they evaluate agents that use their MCP tools and skills, using critical user journey (CUJ) based evals. They argue unit tests can't show whether an agent picks and sequences tools correctly, so they run natural-language CUJs with simulated multi-turn users, grade both the tool-call path and the real cloud resource end state, use deterministic checks before structured LLM-judge scorecards calibrated against humans, and reset real resources between runs. The takeaway is that evals expose silent regressions from harness changes (tool search, skill truncation), justify or retire skills via ablation, and showed long-running operations should move to MCP tasks rather than agent polling; their framework EvalBench is open source.

description:
Agents look impressive in a demo, then quietly get worse after a small change to a prompt, tool, or skill. In this talk, Kurtis Van Gent and Haoyu Wang of Google Cloud Databases explain how to test an AI agent on real user journeys so you catch breaks before your users do. They share lessons from building EvalBench, an open-source evaluation framework that grew from NL2SQL testing into complex agent workflows.

Kurtis is an MCP core maintainer and leads the transport working group. Kurtis and Haoyu both work on Google Cloud Databases.

Topics covered:
- Why unit tests fall short: They confirm that code runs, but not whether an agent uses the tool correctly, in the right order, with the right result.
- Critical user journeys (CUJs): Tasks written the way a user would ask for them, such as "Show me my top customers," not as instructions to call a specific tool. The same evals run against Claude Code, Codex, and other agents.
- Multi-turn journeys: A simulated user answers follow-up questions, such as which region matters, so the agent is tested across the whole conversation.
- Grading the path and the outcome: Check which tools were called, in what order, whether extra calls were made, and whether the cloud resources ended up in the expected state.
- Explainable LLM judges: Use deterministic checks first, such as running a golden query and comparing the data. Use structured scorecards for the rest, and calibrate them against human raters.

analysis.summary: A conference talk by Dmitry Petrov (creator of DVC, founder of DataChain) on building a semantic/context layer so data agents can reason over millions of unstructured files in S3-style object storage. He frames three problems (context window limits, compute to extract information, and trusting saved results) and demos a Slack-fronted Claude Code agent that reuses a previously computed, versioned dataset to answer a video-quality question in about 3 minutes instead of ~30 minutes of compute. The takeaway is that agents should continuously populate a typed, lineage-aware knowledge base and pair it with 'trust machinery' that verifies cached results against current data before answering.

description:
Data agents need more than file access. Dmitry Petrov, creator of the open source tool DVC and founder of DataChain, explains how to build the semantic layer that lets an AI agent understand what is inside the files in an S3 bucket. Without that layer, an agent rebuilds the same understanding from zero on every question, and every follow-up repeats the full compute cost. This talk shows how to save each pass as a typed, versioned dataset that other agents can reuse.

Join us at AGNTCon + MCPCon NA 2026, the premier event for people building, operating, researching, or supporting agent systems. Where developers, architects, and AI practitioners come together to explore the latest in agentic AI, tool protocols, and production-ready MCP architectures. Learn more here: https://events.linuxfoundation.org/agntcon-mcpcon-north-america/

Key topics
- Why raw files need a context layer: no schema, no lineage, and no semantic layer, just bytes and paths.
- The three problems: context window limits, the compute needed to extract information, and whether you can trust saved results.
- Listing and syncing millions of S3 objects, and why agents default to slow, costly scans.
- Reusing saved results: a live demo where a question took about 3 minutes instead of roughly 30 minutes of compute.
- Checking saved answers: duplicates and changed data can make a cached result wrong.
- Exposing datasets over MCP so several agents share the same state.

Instead of only guarding inputs and outputs with judge models or a classifier for every failure, he learns a baseline from normal traffic and flags KV pages that look unusual, catching problems like a hidden spoken instruction in a voicemail where there is no text to filter. In this episode of Build It, I show you a hidden developer mode I built into our smart personal trainer app in an afternoon, without writing any code. It's a custom Component Inspector: any part of the app can be loaded on its own, switched into any state with one-click presets, and checked against natural language tests, with no need to replay the whole flow or burn extra Gemini API calls.

You'll see how I built it with Google Antigravity: starting with a single component, getting that one right, then having Gemini turn the process into reusable skills and a rule for an "inspector mode." That mode keeps the inspector in sync while you work. Then we put it to the test live, adding an error state with a retry button, an expandable view of the workout you're editing, and a cleaner, auto-expanding chat input.

description:
**Most AI agents ship on a hunch: someone runs a few prompts, decides the answers look fine, and releases it. Laurie Voss, Head of Developer Relations at Arize AI and co-founder of NPM Inc., shows how to replace that guesswork with agent evals: repeatable tests that return real numbers on whether your agent got better or worse, and whether a new model is worth switching to.**

What this talk covers:
- Why vibes fail: Three good-looking runs is not a test suite. A prompt change can fix the tone and quietly break something you never tested.
- Traces and evals: Traces are the logs of what your agent did. Evals are the tests that judge whether the result was any good.
- MCP vs CLI, tested with data: For managing a GitHub repo, both approaches were equally correct. On the hardest tasks, MCP cost six times more and took five times as long.
- Three kinds of evals: Code checks for hard rules, LLM judges for meaning, and humans for new failure types and for checking the judges.
- Why agents are harder to test: One early mistake carries through every later step, and an agent can write a confident report on the wrong subject, such as a search for Tesla returning pages about the inventor.
- Pass@k vs pass^k: A demo only has to work once. Production has to work every time.
- Read traces before writing evals: Label real failures, rank them by frequency times severity, and write rules from what you find.
- Building a judge that works: Give it a role, explicit criteria, clearly marked data,
title: Stop Vibe-Testing: Run Real Agent Evals - Laurie Voss, Arize AI

description:
A coding agent wired unit tests to production inference, then ran them about 30 times. Keiji Kanazawa had spent three weeks letting coding agents refactor a personal research assistant. A bad digest sent him looking for a trace, and he discovered the "agent" was still a deterministic workflow. Skills had no SKILL.md, different architectural concepts were aliases for the same thing, and a daily reflection job was producing empty reports. He had approved plans without checking whether the implementation meant what its labels promised.

He rebuilt around an explicit agent runtime, clearer specifications and goal rubrics, comparing four frameworks before selecting tools for his own needs as a product manager. The working example is a video deep dive agent that extracts 440 keyframes from an inference lecture, pairs blackboard equations with explanations and lets him question individual sections. The result generalizes to slide decks, coding demos and terminal recordings. He iterates on an evaluation rubric, lets agents optimize against it and uses adversarial reviews between coding agents. The rubrics need scrutiny too: one was tuned to a single lecture and failed on five other videos. His answer to the code reading debate is to own the goals and evaluation loop while continuing to delegate most implementation.

description:
Tanmay Sah and Dolly Sah look at a capability today's coding agents are missing: undoing what they've done. Drawing on their research projects UndoBench and EvoUndo, they show that an agent that completes a task can't necessarily put things back when something breaks, because Git doesn't cover external API calls, runtime config or notifications, and retrying doesn't reverse side effects. In EvoUndo, 197 of 478 changes that made an agent more capable (about 42%) also broke its ability to recover. They lay out an approach that captures the original state, picks the right response (retry, restore, compensate or escalate) and independently verifies the result.

description:
If ChatGPT ignores parts of your MCP server, slows down when it uses your tools, or rejects your plugin submission, this keynote has the fixes. Thomas Sarlandie of OpenAI's plugins team shares what developers get wrong when they build MCP servers for ChatGPT, using OpenAI's data on how people use MCP in its public plugin directory. The talk was given at AGNTCon + MCPCon North America 2026, the conference for people building, operating, and supporting agent systems.

What the talk covers
- Tool count: There is no limit on how many tools you expose to the model. Developers already expose hundreds of tools, so do not cap yourself at 5 or 10.
- Schema size: Very large schemas, some in the megabyte range, get trimmed by ChatGPT. Review your schema by hand, and do not paste whole skills into tool descriptions, because they will be cut off.
- The list-and-run trap: Exposing only two generic tools, one to list commands and one to run them, hides your real tools from the model, from client builders, and from enterprise admins who want to control access.
- Tool annotations: Mark every tool as read-only or destructive. ChatGPT auto-approves read-only tools, so they run faster. Destructive tools get extra checks and need the user's explicit approval. Plugin submissions without annotations on all tools are rejected.
- Server instructions: Only 56 percent of plugins in the public directory use them. OpenAI's documentation recommends no more than 500 characters, and up to about 1,000 is fin
title: The Key to Creating GREAT OpenAI Plugins- Thomas Sarlandie, OpenAI

description:
Stuffing raw chat history into a prompt isn't a memory strategy. Here is how to give AI agents persistent memory across sessions while cutting classifier token usage by 86%. In this episode of AI Agent Clinic, Google Cloud AI engineer Laxmi Harikumar and developer Miles Libbey take Scribant, an open source voice to action agent built with the Agent Development Kit (ADK) in Gemini platform, and combine 3 memory and context harness patterns in 60 minutes: persistent memory with Memory Bank, a 40 word rolling window, and rolling summary compaction.

🔗 Repositories & resources:
* Scribant Agent Code (GitHub) → https://g.dev/ai/scribant-agent
* Agent Development Kit (ADK) docs → https://g.dev/ai/adk
* Memory Bank in Gemini platform (Vertex AI) docs → https://g.dev/ai/memory-bank
* Google Antigravity → https://goo.gle/3R5gUki

Scribant listens every 2 seconds and turns spoken thoughts into Google Calendar events, tasks, and Jira tickets. Sending the full transcript on every speech tick burned tokens, spiked latency, and still left the agent with no memory once the app closed. Here are the 3 harness patterns in action:
* *Pattern 1, Memory Bank (Vertex AI):* asynchronously extracts, deduplicates, and resolves conflicting user facts across sessions, injecting just 24 tokens of distilled memory instead of roughly 1,400 raw RAG tokens.
* *Pattern 2, 40 word rolling window:* rule based compaction that feeds the intent classifier only the latest 40 words instead of 10 lines of transcript
title: Why your AI agent keeps forgetting (and getting slower)

analysis.summary: Harald Kirschner from the VS Code team presents the Agent Host Protocol (AHP), an open Microsoft spec that moves agent sessions out of a single app into a host process that many clients can connect to. He demos a plan started in VS Code, continued in the Agents window, and opened via vscode.dev on a phone against a remote dev box, then covers snapshots, replay, first-writer-wins conflict handling, sub-agents as separate chats, MCP state sync, and automations. description:
**Harald Kirschner from Microsoft explains why an AI agent's work gets trapped in the chat window where it started, and how the open Agent Host Protocol (AHP) lets one running session be watched, reviewed, and steered from a laptop, a remote dev box, or a phone. If you have ever waited on an agent that needed your approval while you were away from your computer, this talk shows the fix.**

Topics covered:
- Why sessions get stuck: agents now run for hours, edit files, run terminals, and ask for approval, but each session lives inside one app.
- Standards that worked before: how the Language Server Protocol (LSP) let every editor reuse the same language tooling, and why agents need the same pattern.
- Skills, AGENTS.md, and MCP: shared standards for agent know-how, repository instructions, and tool connections.
- A host that owns the session: a dedicated agent host keeps the live session running, even when the laptop lid closes.
- Multi-client demo: start a plan in VS Code, continue it in the Agents window, and open the same session in a browser on a phone.
- Snapshots and replay: a client that joins gets the full conversation and workspace state, and a reconnecting client replays what it missed.
- Sub-agents and automations: background sub-agents appear as separate chats, and automations can run on the host with no client connected.
- AHP compared with ACP and A2A: many clients to one host (AHP), one agent inside one editor (ACP), and agents handing work to other agents (A2A)
title: The Agent Has Left the Chat - Harald Kirschner, Microsoft

description:
A customer call ended with a bug, and an agent found the unfinished task in the transcript and screen recording. In Prasanna Sankar's account, it asked for permission to investigate, involved the responsible engineer, produced a pull request and drafted the customer followup after the fix shipped. That example captures where Vorflux's engineering work led: once agents can complete longer tasks, coordinating and starting the right work becomes its own bottleneck. Prasanna traces the progression from cloud coding sessions to persistent bots with a goal, an owner and a shared channel.

The foundation is six practical problems: reproducing a working development environment, investing more effort in planning, dividing tasks with dependencies, testing without returning to a laptop, reviewing from multiple angles, and keeping changes mergeable as the base branch moves. Browser tests, recordings and staging links give people something concrete to inspect. The second half shifts from those coding workflows to on call, CI and project management bots that respond to signals already present in the company. Prasanna also describes the failure mode of indiscriminate automation: noisy alerts, unwanted pull requests and growing token bills. His proposed controls are budgets, visible work, named ownership and increasing responsibility as results justify it. These are lessons and examples from building Vorflux, with a clear acknowledgment that the bots remain fallible and some responsibilities
title: Merge Is the Bottleneck - Prasanna Sankar, Vorflux

description:
Most AI agents fail in production because a single prompt can’t guarantee order, safety checks, or human approval. Today, we’re building a fully autonomous, multimodal AI video studio from scratch using Google’s Agent Development Kit.

Imagine running a daily cozy-spooky video channel ("VibeTube"). Every night, your audience sends you chaotic ideas: voice notes, porch videos, spooky photos, and text comments. Gemini can read them, Imagen can draw the posters, and Veo can render the video.

The problem? Generative models can do the chores, but they can’t run the studio. They can't refuse a bad idea before it burns your API budget, pause for your approval, or wait for a slow video render without timing out. A prompt can’t promise order. A workflow graph can.

In this live build, we are walking through the VibeStudio (Haunted Edition), architecture to turn a chaotic creative process into a deterministic, production ready ADK Workflow on Google Cloud.

*What the team is building live:*
* 🧠 Beyond basic prompts: Moving from single turn agents to structured ADK Workflow graphs (fan-out, parallel JoinNodes, and smart routers).
* 👁️ Multimodal RAG ingestion: Using Gemini to transcribe voice notes, caption photos, and watch video clips—feeding them all into a single Vertex AI RAG Engine corpus.
* 🛑 The 2 types of suspension: How to make your agent pause for a human-in-the-loop decision and asynchronously wait on long running Veo video renders without holding connections open.

description:
An official diagnostic skill can read cloud credentials, contact identity services and probe an instance metadata endpoint. Those same actions can resemble an information stealer. Roey Ben Chaim of Zenity and the MATS Fellowship uses that ambiguity to explain why reading a SKILL.md file cannot establish what an agent will actually do. Instructions can fetch more instructions, installation scripts can pull in packages, and those packages can create processes whose effects never appear in the agent's own trace. The missing evidence is runtime behavior, collected inside a controlled environment.

Roey walks through the evolution of an agent detonation chamber: a sandbox, a world builder that supplies the services a skill expects, an operator that exercises different paths, and instrumentation for processes, filesystem activity and network traffic. He then follows concrete cases involving chained skill installation, a misleading package name, persistence, hooks and remotely fetched prompts. One investigation traces a lookalike project through a downloaded payload to credential harvesting, showing why the complete chain matters more than the entry file. The examples illustrate both malicious behavior and legitimate activity that can trigger suspicion; they are not a claim that one scanner can classify every skill correctly. The engineering takeaway is to treat skills as software dependencies, inspect what they load, restrict their access, and preserve evidence of what executes bey
title: You Can't Tell What an Agent Skill Will Do by Reading It - Roey Ben Chaim, Zenity

description:
Twelve alerts fire at 2 a.m., and a useful assistant can still leave the engineer coordinating every step. Meta's on call team uses that illustrative scenario to explain a different design: one AI teammate per rotation, with shared context, its own identity, persistent memory and explicit limits on what it can do. Swaapnika Motapothula, Chinmay Gandhi and Vlad Tsvang describe a system that connects alerts, tickets, incident history and code changes instead of leaving each automation with its own isolated view. The goal is to bring a human a decision with supporting evidence and a proposed action.

Their autonomy ladder starts with investigation, advances to drafting fixes for approval, and permits selected lower criticality work only when mistakes are cheap to detect and the agent has earned trust on that action. Critical production decisions stay with people, and code changes still go through normal review and continuous integration. The team explains the automation loops for triage, recovery from stuck runs, and shift handoffs, plus how team specific skills and memory carry expertise between engineers. Corrections reopen work and become new evidence, while memory entries can be promoted or retired. The examples show the intended experience rather than a measured time savings result: the speakers explicitly reserve that claim for a rigorous study. Their next steps focus on accepted mitigations, better feedback and earning further autonomy.

title: Give Your On-Call Its Own AI Teammate - Swaapnika Motapothula, Chinmay Gandhi & Vlad Tsvang, Meta

analysis.applies_to_work: The consent model is moving from a user clicking 'approve' to admin-managed connections and agent-owned identities, so AX approval UI needs new patterns: an admin console for one-time MCP server connection, and end-user views that show which agent identity acted and within what scope (e.g. workspace or channel claims). In an AI component library, the tool-call and approval components should be able to display agent identity, token scope and expiry rather than only a per-call confirm button. For developer portals, the auth story maps cleanly onto doc pages: an IdP integration guide, a token passthrough anti-pattern page, audience and issuer validation checklists, and a conformance and SDK-tier status page.

Conformance tests as an enforceable contract, with roughly a third of scenarios security-focused
Why the 'person clicks approve' consent model no longer scales for long-running agents
Enterprise-managed auth: admin connects once, users never see consent prompts
Workload authorization grant as the path to agent identity with policy claims

analysis.relevance_reason: The shift from per-user consent prompts to admin-managed and agent-identity authorization directly reshapes the consent, delegation and trust UI Parag designs for agentic experiences and developer portals, though the talk itself is protocol-level rather than design-focused.
analysis.summary: A conference talk by Den Delimarsky, an MCP lead maintainer at Anthropic, reviewing nearly two years of MCP security across three pillars: the protocol spec, the official SDKs, and deployment best practices. He traces MCP's move from do-it-yourself auth to an opinionated OAuth 2.1 model with external identity providers, then covers SDK conformance testing and coordinated disclosure. The main takeaway is that MCP is moving from human-in-the-loop consent prompts to agent-first authorization through enterprise-managed auth, DPoP, workload identity federation and workload authorization grants that give agents their own short-lived, policy-bearing identity.

description:
Den Delimarsky of Anthropic explains how to keep AI agents and the tools they connect to secure, based on two years of running the Model Context Protocol (MCP) in production. If you build MCP servers or clients, or run AI agents that touch your email, sales data, or other accounts, this talk shows which security decisions matter most and why.

The talk follows three parts of MCP security: the protocol specification, the official SDKs, and security best practices for deploying servers.

What the talk covers
- Authorization on standard OAuth: why MCP chose OAuth 2.1 and how enterprise identity providers take over sign-in and token management.
- Consent and confused deputy risks: why per-client consent matters and how a server can end up approving the wrong thing.
- Token handling: avoiding token passthrough, and validating the audience and issuer of tokens to prevent mix-up attacks.
- SDK security: how coordinated vulnerability disclosure works across the SDKs and why conformance tests enforce security rules.
- Consent without a person clicking: enterprise-managed authorization, proof-of-possession tokens (DPoP), and workload identity federation.
- Agent identity: how workload authorization grants give agents short-lived tokens with policy claims, instead of shared static credentials.

This talk is for MCP server and client developers, and for anyone responsible for deploying agents in an organization.

0:40 The three pi
title: MCP Security, Two Years In - Den Delimarsky, Anthropic

If you run a website or app, AI agents are already trying to use it, and most of them do it the slow way: reading screenshots and guessing at buttons. Frédéric Barthelet, CTO and co-founder of Alpic, and Dominic Farolino, a Google Chrome engineer and one of the authors of WebMCP, show three ways to give agents a proper way in: MCP servers, WebMCP, and command line tools.

They demo each one live, then walk through how to choose based on who uses your product and what they need to do.

Topics covered:

- Agent experience (AX): Why being found by an agent is only half the job. It also has to sign in for the user and finish the task.
- Agents are already users: Cloudflare reported in 2026 that bot traffic passed human traffic, largely driven by AI agents.
- MCP: The original capability layer, where agents connect to tools in the background and you stay in the agent's interface.
- WebMCP: Tools live on the web page itself, so you and your agent use the same site and the agent skips the screenshots and page scraping.
- Command line tools: Agents reuse a CLI you already have installed and signed in to.
- Agent environments: How browser, shell, and server access shape which option an agent can use at all.
- Visual feedback: When people need to see the page, and when terminal output is enough.
- Access control: Why MCP is the only option with a standard authorization path, OAuth 2.1.
- Distribution: Search for the web, pack

analysis.applies_to_work: Precision before recall is a direct AX principle: agent notification, finding and approval components should only surface high-confidence items, and silently dropped items should stay auditable (a 'judge reviewed X dropped findings' disclosure). Address rate is a trust metric worth adding to the AI component library: instrument accept, dismiss and act actions on agent suggestion cards and tool-call approval UI. The reviewer, coordinator and judge chain suggests a provenance or citation pattern that shows why a finding survived, for example 'checked against the feature flag config'. For developer portals, risk-tier badges that decide how much human review a change gets are a concrete pattern to prototype.

analysis.relevance_reason: The precision-over-recall principle, the multi-agent filtering chain, and the address-rate trust metric map directly onto how Parag designs agent supervision, trust and approval UI, though the talk is about code review rather than design systems.
analysis.summary: A conference talk by Joah Gerstenberg, a tech lead at Block, on rebuilding the company's AI code reviewer so developers actually trust and act on its findings. He argues that verification is now the bottleneck, that reviewers must be measured offline against a labeled corpus of expert reviews, and that precision must come before recall, using parallel specialist reviewers, a coordinator that tries to disprove findings, a judge, and risk-based routing to control cost. The main takeaway is that trust in agentic systems comes from measurement, protecting human attention by posting only high-confidence findings, and aligning agents with business context before code is written.

description:
Engineering teams now have agents writing code faster than people can review it. When an AI reviewer posts too many wrong findings, people stop reading what it says. In this talk, Joah Gerstenberg of Block, Inc. explains how Block rebuilt its AI code reviewer to favor precision, so the comments that reach developers are ones worth acting on.

Topics covered:
- Verification as the bottleneck: once models could write trustworthy code, checking that code became the hard part.
- Code review as a ritual of trust: reviewers at Block now handle about three times as many lines of code as they did a year ago.
- Measuring against human reviews: a test corpus of expert reviews sets the bar, but human comments are not what the model should copy.
- The worst comment: an April bug exposed the reviewer's learned behavior, and Block shut the reviewer down for a week to rebuild it.
- Precision before recall: fewer, correct findings earn trust, and the address rate rose as precision improved.
- Specialist reviewers and a judge: several reviewers inspect a change, a coordinator tries to disprove their findings, and a judge reviews what was dropped.
- Risk-based routing: low-risk changes get a cheaper review and high-risk changes get a deeper one, based on privacy, security, money movement, and SOX compliance.
- Open source: block/review follows this architecture with six review agents.
- Alignment and containment: agents need the wider business context, and the talk also covers Buzz, Block's op

description:
A pull request can claim that checks passed even when the recorded commands do not establish that the submitted change was tested. Cassandra Chin built Tracetoon to recover the context behind a branch, write a better pull request description and optionally explain it with a comic. Together with Stephen Chin, she follows one troublesome review through repeated revisions, missing evidence and rising token costs. The problem is more specific than producing fluent prose: the writer needs to connect a change to its rationale, the commands that ran, their timing and the version of the code they actually checked.

Their next iteration uses Relate, an embedded graph database written in Rust, to assemble that evidence before the writing begins. A connected brief gives the writer and reviewers the same sources, reducing repeated searches through session logs. The speakers explain why they kept a stronger writer while using less expensive reviewers to check claims against the brief, and show results from their own PR Bench development comparisons. Those reported results combine improved description quality with roughly half the token usage; they describe this project's evaluation, not a guarantee for other codebases. The practical pattern is to preserve provenance and relationships outside the model's conversation, make uncertainty visible, and give reviewers evidence tied to the submitted content. The comic provides the story, but the useful engineering artifact is the reviewable chain
title: Your PR Says the Tests Passed. Prove It. - Stephen Chin & Cassandra Chin

If you run AI agents, you are probably keeping a machine on for weeks or months to get a few minutes of real work done. Clare Liguori, Senior Principal Engineer at AWS working on the Kiro coding assistant and a core maintainer of the Model Context Protocol (MCP), shows how reactive agents fix that: they only run when there is work to do, so idle time costs nothing.

She shares results from Infinity, an experimental project at Amazon that fit 75,000 hibernating agents into the memory of a Raspberry Pi, then walks through what MCP needs to support this pattern.

Topics covered:

- Why agents mostly wait: A tool takes 15 minutes to finish, a person replies next week, or an alert does not arrive for a month.
- The always-on problem: Most agent frameworks hold a process open the whole time, including the Mac mini Clare keeps running for one agent.
- What a reactive agent is: A running process only while it has work to do. The rest of the time it is just data, like a row in a database or a file on disk.
- Three properties: The agent can suspend and resume, work continues while it hibernates, and an outside event can wake it.
- Inside Infinity: Agents run as short execution slices, with no stack in memory and no open connections between them.
- Multi-round trip requests: How the latest MCP spec removes the long-lived streams that kept agents awake.
- The MCP tasks extension: Start slow work like provisioning a database, get a task ID, and sleep u
title: Your Agent Doesn't Need to Be Always On

Building an AI agent that turns messy spoken thoughts into Google Calendar events, tasks, and dev tickets? Here is how Scribant's 3 stage Agent Development Kit (ADK) pipeline works: Stage 1 uses Google Cloud Speech to Text for fast transcription with zero LLM overhead; Stage 2 runs two specialist ADK agents side by side (rolling summary + action extraction) with a deterministic date resolver so the model never guesses calendar math; and Stage 3 wraps everything in a strictly read only Execution Gate so nothing touches your Google Calendar or dev workspace until you click approve. This 3 stage system worked for single sessions, until multi day use broke everything. Watch the full Episode 4 fix linked below the title.

Watch the full episode on the Google Cloud Tech channel and let us know what you think.

description:
An agent can hide a failed test behind a successful shell pipeline. It can also trim away the error message and confidently report that everything worked. Ayush Bhardwaj examined roughly 20,000 tool calls from his own coding sessions and found a product roadmap in the commands agents wrote immediately afterward. Repeated uses of head, tail, grep and Python showed where tools returned too much information, exposed the wrong fields, or made the agent reconstruct the same query again. The examples come from his own traces and his chat history CLI, which lets agents retrieve context from earlier coding sessions.

The fixes are small and concrete: return the messages around a search match, offer compact search results, inspect several sessions in one call, and put a useful failure summary at the end of the output. But implementing a flag does little if the skill file still teaches the old interface. In Ayush's case study, agents kept passing a flag that did nothing until the instructions changed. He also explains how to turn recorded calls into replay tests, reserve examples for evaluation, and check whether better output actually improves answers and reduces turns. Smaller responses alone do not establish a faster or cheaper workflow. The useful feedback is already in the transcript: what the agent tried, what it discarded, and what it had to ask again.

description:
Here is what most people get wrong about AI memory: they save the chat transcript. That is not memory. That is a log.

Real memory has to separate two different things:
• Facts (your name, your budget) → exact values that belong in a database
• Meaning (“I like quiet, minimal things”) → understanding that belongs in vector memory

That is the difference. Episode 5 shows how to design that memory system for any AI agent, using a live bidirectional multimodal agent as the example.

description:
TorchTPU is an open-source, native PyTorch backend for Google Cloud TPUs, built by Google in collaboration with the PyTorch team at Meta. With TorchTPU, you can run standard PyTorch code on TPUs by setting device = torch.device("tpu") (or device = torch.accelerator.current_accelerator()), then debug in eager mode, compile with torch.compile, and scale from a single chip to a multi-host slice with torch.distributed.

In this video, we walk through how TorchTPU integrates with the PyTorch dispatcher, StableHLO, and the XLA compiler, and run a live demo on a Cloud TPU v6e (Trillium) chip in both eager and compiled modes. We also cover multi-chip scaling through the standard PyTorch process group API (tpu_dist) and integrations across the open-source ecosystem, including Hugging Face Transformers, TorchTitan, vLLM, SGLang, Ray, and llm-d.

description:
A Rust program can compile and still violate the decisions an experienced teammate would catch immediately. Brian Douglas finds that missing knowledge in moments when engineers push back on their coding agents. At Paper Compute, he captures agent sessions, labels corrections and uses those traces to recover the reasoning that otherwise disappears inside a local coding harness. His example starts with a gap in his own Rust expertise: accepting plausible generated code leads to objections later, when a teammate reviews the pull request. Those earlier objections become useful training material only if someone preserves and labels them.

Brian demonstrates session capture with Tapes and Paper Console, then runs a Twin Review prototype against a pull request using examples of a teammate's feedback. He discusses labels for pushback, successful sessions and regressions, and shows how the same records can support skills, evaluations or model adaptation. The prototype is a demonstration, not a measured comparison against an independent evaluation set, and Brian corrects himself during the recording to clarify that Twin Review is not publicly released because its data is sensitive. His practical starting point is simpler than training a model: collect the traces you already generate, find the corrections that encode your team's conventions, and turn those into a skill you can test. The durable asset is the connection between a decision, the expert's objection and the resulting outcome.
title: Every Correction You Give Your Agent Is Data - Brian Douglas, Paper Compute

description:
A biopharma automation reached 99.95% accuracy on its business critical tasks after the team separated actual errors from ambiguous cases and exceptions. Matthew Jewkes describes building that system at Clarivate, where indexing drug development documents meant handling tens of thousands of new tasks a month. An early agent approach reached around 80% to 83%. Working through 1,000 evaluation examples with domain experts exposed three different problems: the model could be wrong, the organization could lack an agreed answer, or genuinely new science could require judgment. Each needed its own route. The routine path became a tightly specified automation, with uncertain and unusual cases escalated instead of pushed through.

The larger payoff was recovering expert attention. Once routine decisions were handled, the remaining cases could be grouped for deliberate review: critical exceptions to clear, ambiguous low value work to freeze, and unusual demand that might justify a new product. One expert used that structured backlog to form an investment thesis before a major customer raised the same need. Jewkes lays out where the investment makes sense, how much evaluation work high reliability requires and why organizational ownership and trust matter alongside engineering. His bet is that companies will gain more from managing collective attention and judgment than from choosing a particular orchestration framework.

description:
Multi-Agent SRE: What Happens When Your Agents Want Opposite Things - Aditi Mewada, Apple

As SRE teams adopt multi-agent systems, a new class of problem emerges: agents with conflicting objectives operating on the same infrastructure at the same time. Your remediation agent wants to spin up three new nodes to absorb a traffic spike. Your cost-optimization agent wants to terminate underutilized instances to hit budget targets. Both are correct. Both are about to make things worse.

This talk explores the real-world failure modes of multi-agent SRE systems - what happens when agents act on stale state, override each other's changes, or reach a deadlock - and how to design your way out of it. We'll cover conflict detection, priority hierarchies, shared state management, and when to hand control back to a human.
You'll leave with practical patterns for building multi-agent systems that disagree productively, rather than destructively.
title: Multi-Agent SRE: What Happens When Your Agents Want Opposite Things - Aditi Mewada, Apple

description:
Do more AI agents always mean better results? Not always, it depends on what you're building and how your agents work together.

When building an app with AI, adding more agents comes with real trade-offs:
• Majority voting (asking multiple agents to fix the same bug) → helps surface consensus, but the most popular answer can still be wrong
• Agent teams (splitting UI, data, and testing across specialized agents) → can run tasks in parallel to finish faster and catch missed bugs
• Sequential handoffs (agents building on each other's work) → one early mistake can cascade down the chain

An agent team can help you explore ideas, move faster, and catch bugs, just remember that more agents doesn't automatically mean a better answer.

#AIAgents #MultiAgentSystems #AIDevelopment #SoftwareEngineering #LLM #GoogleCloud

title: More AI agents = better results?

analysis.summary: A short AI Engineer talk by Nikolay Petrov (Intel) on measuring what an agent skill (SKILL.md) actually teaches a model versus what the model already knows. He splits a skill into ~25–30 checkable items (propositions or contracts with Q&A pairs), runs each with and without the skill, and uses an LLM judge to sort items into already-known, harmful, newly taught, or still-missed. The takeaway: most skill content is redundant general knowledge, while the real value sits in exact details (keys, parameters, values), so use this novelty map as a starting vector for trimming, then confirm with task-level evals.

description:
Adding a line to a skill takes seconds, but removing one is scary, so skills only grow. Nikolay Petrov shows how to see inside a skill: split it into small checkable claims, test the model with and without each one, and get a line-by-line map of what the skill actually teaches, what the model already knew, and what makes it worse. The first skill they tested was 70% things the model already knew. The value was in the other 30%, the exact details a naive shortener would cut first.

analysis.summary: This is the day-one livestream of MCP Dev Summit Nairobi 2026 (Agentic AI Foundation), covering keynotes on agent safety in African digital health, the stateless MCP spec, and Anthropic's global-health MCP work, plus breakout talks on FHIR+MCP clinical workflows, small-model tool design, MCP auth, tool-poisoning prompt injection, server-side data boundaries, legacy systems, OpenTelemetry observability, and a voice-agent MCP over a national credential registry. The recurring argument is that an agent's ability to act does not grant it authority to act, so permissions, human-in-the-loop approval, traceability, reversibility and policy enforcement must live in the MCP server and tool design rather than in the model. The main takeaway is that MCP is maturing (stateless core, OAuth profile, MCP Apps) and that shipping an MCP server means shipping expertise and guardrails, with security boundaries enforced deterministically server-side.

description:
Cameron Wolfe, a staff research scientist at Netflix and author of the Deep (Learning) Focus newsletter, lays out a three-part framework for evaluating tasks with no single right answer, like creative writing. Human evaluation with calibrated guidelines is the North Star; LLM judges and rubrics, checked against human "golden" data, scale up offline evals; and A/B tests and production monitoring confirm results in the real world. Along the way he covers fighting noise with power analysis, error bars and resampling, and a Netflix project where an LLM judge's scores were causally linked to viewers abandoning shows.
